summary: Earth Change Explorer is an interactive web tool that helps anyone see what's changing in Earth's environment, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. We built it to address the challenge of selecting and analysing Earth science variables that trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another. It combines NASA MODIS vegetation greenness and NASA GISS surface temperature with sea ice, precipitation, ocean and atmospheric datasets. Users can choose a variable, region, season and period, then explore trends on a 3D globe and flat map, plus regional time series tested with Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope. The 'Compare Regions' tool flags regions trending in opposite directions, and the 'Discover' tool scans every variable in every region, controls the false discovery rate, and ranks the greatest and most contrasting changes. It matters because Earth data is overwhelming, and misread statistics lead to poor decisions: this tool makes significance visible and helps non-experts decide what deserves attention.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The user picks an Earth science variable, a region, a season, and a time period. The tool averages monthly gridded data into annual or seasonal values, then computes a trend and p-value at every grid cell. Results are shown on a 3D globe and a flat map, with non-significant areas dimmed. A selected region is area-weighted (cosine of latitude) into one time series and tested with Mann-Kendall (significance) and Sen's slope (size per decade); autocorrelation-corrected versions (Hamed-Rao, Yue-Wang) are available. The Compare tab tests two regions side by side and flags opposite significant trends. The Discover tab tests every variable in every preset region and lists the greatest changes and the strongest opposite-trend pairs. Plain-language summaries explain every result.

BENEFITS

It lowers the barrier to trend analysis for students, teachers, and non-specialists, shows statistical significance visibly instead of hiding it, and helps users choose which variables are worth investigating.

INTENDED IMPACT

Help students and communities understand environmental change, and help researchers quickly find regions where a variable trends in opposite directions.

TOOLS

Python, Streamlit, xarray, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall, Plotly, earthaccess, pyhdf, Google Colab, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud. Data came from NASA MODIS (MOD13C2), NASA GISS (GISTEMP), and NOAA, GPCP, NCEP/NCAR, and JMA datasets, all listed in the references except False discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_discovery_rate, which wasn't included in the references due to the limit being reached.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It treats the challenge's problem (too many variables, trends that reverse between regions, unclear significance) as a discovery problem: Discover scans everything and surfaces opposite-trend pairs automatically, and the globe makes significance visible at a glance. It also applies false discovery rate control, so the scan does not present chance results as findings.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific validity: autocorrelation-aware tests, multiple-testing correction, and a limitations section. Accessibility: open data that needs no login to explore, plain-language results, a readable dark interface. Performance: coarser grids and compressed data so it runs on free hosting. Honesty: short records, model-based reanalysis variables, correlated neighbouring cells, and a sea ice record that ends in 2019 are all stated in the app. Citations: every data source, library, and font is credited; however, due to the limit on the amount of 'Space Agency Partner & Other Data', I wasn't able to include every source.
